segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Neil Drumming is one of the producers of our show. Coming up, an entire town gets a status update, and they are not super stoked about it. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life . I'm Ira Glass. Each week on the program, of course, we choose a theme, bring you different kinds of stories on that theme. Today's program-- "Status Update."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today's program is about people whose position in the world changes, in one way or another, and how they deal with it. So far on our show, we've had a literal status update, the social media kind. We've heard what it sounds like inside a friendship where there's been a major shift in status.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And now we've arrived at Act Three of our show. Act Three, There Owes the Neighborhood. In this act, we're going to look at an entire city getting a status update. And the man who gave this city the news about itself was named Paul Kiel. Before the city knew, Paul Kiel knew. And before Paul Kiel knew, nobody knew.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Here's what happened. Paul's an investigative reporter with ProPublica. And he discovered that over the last 15 years, this new kind of debt collector has become more prevalent. These are companies that go after people who owe on their credit cards, or car loans, or hospital bills, or whatever.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And these companies, what they do is they garnish people's wages. They garnish their wages. They take the money right out of their paychecks. Sometimes they go straight into their bank accounts and take the money.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They got this power by taking these people to court. Way more consumers who owe money are being taken to court. These companies sue those consumers, which used to be rare. They sue, and they win. And because they win, they get the power to garnish these wages.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so figuring out that part was just the beginning. Chana Joffe-Walt talked to Paul Kiel.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It was a struggle to get numbers on wage garnishing. How many people? How much money? Where were those people? Paul Kiel loves this kind of thing. He's an even-measured guy who enjoys the grunt work of tracking down which file cabinet in which municipal building of which small town has the information he needs.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Eventually, Paul and his colleague Annie Waldman had managed to track down the names and addresses of every single person who'd been sued for not paying their debts in three cities-- Newark, Chicago, and St. Louis. They put all that information into the computer, and then Paul looked at what they had.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: Without doing a fancy analysis, if we sorted our neighborhoods so that the ones that had the most lawsuits were at the top, it was all black neighborhoods.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: In Newark, Chicago--

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: In Newark and Chicago and in St. Louis.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: All of them.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: All of them.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So there were way more lawsuits in black neighborhoods than in white neighborhoods.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: Yes. That was clear no matter how you looked at it. In neighborhoods that had the same income level, the same household income, on average, we were finding twice as many lawsuits in the mostly black neighborhoods. And then it was a real question of why.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Paul knew people would look at this and think what I thought. This is just discrimination-- companies targeting black people and black neighborhoods.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did you think this was just racism?

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: No, I didn't. No, I didn't jump to that conclusion, just because I know how it's such a large and impersonal system. You know, debt-buying companies and other banks might never meet their customers. You're literally a name on a spreadsheet to these companies. So it was immediately like a puzzle that we needed to find an answer to.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Paul's first clue to the answer came when he went to a place called Jennings, Missouri. Jennings is a suburb of St. Louis, home to an astonishing amount of wage garnishing. And Jennings is where Paul met Cori Winfield.

segments.speaker: Cori Winfield
segments.text: Oh my god. OK, so like an example.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Cori was the first person to show Paul her paycheck. She works for a brokerage services firm in St. Louis.

segments.speaker: Cori Winfield
segments.text: I just got paid Friday. And my check is usually, gross, around $1,100, $1,200, something like that. But when I got my-- when I got paid Friday, I had $691 on my check. My rent is $750.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Here's how this happened. Cori was married-- four kids and a neat brick bungalow under a shady tree with a patch of grass just large enough to be called a lawn. She had a mortgage on that brick bungalow, and she had a van she bought in 2009 for $8,000. The loan on that van is the one that got her in trouble. That's the loan Cori's now paying for out of her paycheck.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So the lender in this case was Midwest Acceptance, which is like a St. Louis-based, mostly subprime auto loan company.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Midwest Acceptance.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: Midwest Acceptance, yes.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Subprime meaning high interest rate. Really high-- 30%. In 2010, Cori stopped paying the car loan. And she stopped paying it for a bunch of reasons. Her husband left, so she had to carry the car loan and the mortgage on the brick bungalow with the small patch of grass all by herself.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Also, Cori's stepfather died. She got a new boyfriend. Her boyfriend was killed. She took a brief absence from work. One of her dogs died. She describes herself at this time as very distracted.

segments.speaker: Cori Winfield
segments.text: So I wasn't keeping up with court dates. I wasn't paying attention to the notices they were sending in the mail.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And they were sending lots of notices. They were calling, too.

segments.speaker: Cori Winfield
segments.text: Midwest Acceptance. And they'd be like, um, when are you going to be in to make a payment? I'll be in, um, on my next pay period.

segments.speaker: Cori Winfield
segments.text: Well, we need you to come in before then.  You're going to have to do something. You don't got a grandma you can call? You don't got a mama you can call? Or little stuff like that.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The grandma. This turned out to be Paul's answer. Cori did have a grandma she often called, but her grandma was already trying to help Cori save her house. And she was helping Cori with car rides once Midwest repo'd Cori's car.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Her grandma was also helping Cori's mom and her uncle. And she was doing all that on a pension. Cori's grandma was the only person she'd ever been able to call in this kind of situation.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: If you ask people, could you borrow $3,000 from a friend or family member in an emergency? White people are much more likely to say yes. Poor whites, a white person living in abject poverty, has roughly the same ability to borrow $3,000 in an emergency as a middle-class black person. That's according to the largest national survey of consumer finance. If you compare Jennings, where Cori was, to white towns where people make the same amount of money?

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: In that income bracket, whites, on average, have five times the wealth as black households.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So wealth meaning home ownership and savings and investments and all of that stuff?

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: It's like everything you have that you could turn into money, whether it be equity in your home, or your car, or whatever. It was right in front of me. So if people in the same income level have five times the wealth, it seems very credible that that would have a major impact on whether they're able to deal with a debt. That, to me, is-- the answer's right there.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: And you were asking me, like, well, is this because of discrimination? And we don't have direct evidence that these suits are happening more often in black communities because of discrimination, but the racial wealth gap is definitely because of discrimination.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: So why do we have a racial wealth gap? Because we had centuries of racist public policy. And even in the 20th century, blacks were prevented from buying homes in certain areas, and there were a lot of policies that helped whites build wealth at the same time they were preventing blacks from doing that. So it was-- it's a wealth gap that was fostered by racist policy, which we really haven't recovered from. Because wealth takes time to build over generations.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Paul knew all of this before he started looking into wage garnishing. He knew this history, from Jim Crow laws all the way up through restrictive covenants in housing. He knew the data. But it wasn't until Cori that he considered it the answer to his puzzle.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Which is interesting. The wealth gap is such a basic old fact about America that it's become a saggy, meaningless phrase. "The widening wealth gap." "How to narrow the wealth gap."

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: It's kind of an abstract concept.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And this is what it looks like.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: Right. Yeah. And so this is one good illustration of that.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: So I'm standing on a street. Standing on a street in the middle of Jennings, not too far from the high school.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Paul found himself in a peculiar situation. He had a detailed spreadsheet, with addresses, listing everyone who hasn't paid their debts, how much they owed, and for what. Basically he had a map of the neighborhood he was standing in that included intimate details about people's financial lives.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: About half the homes on this block have had a lawsuit against them.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: On some blocks, it was every other house. Sometimes there were a few in just one house. It was a social map of the neighborhood that was the opposite of the carefully curated status updates you usually see.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What Paul could see was something real and messy-- what was going on with people's finances. And he wondered, if you live here, do you just know about this? Or do you actually need to see the map to picture it?

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: There's a street-- there's a house at the end here.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: How did you get my name?

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: Well, it was court records.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: So--

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: They are public.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: They are public, yeah. And--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This woman, Devorah, had been sued for money she owed the Metropolitan Sewer District. But she did not know that they'd sued her next door neighbor, too. Up the street and around the corner, Paul finds a block party going on. He sees a guy barbecuing in front of his house, and he knows this guy was sued, too. But the guy doesn't feel like talking about it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The next few people did talk to Paul about it, and the disruption that led to them being sued-- a health incident, a family issue. For Latanya Graves, it was when she lost her job.

segments.speaker: Latanya Graves
segments.text: At the time, I was just trying to get back on my feet. I was laid off from Western Union.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And how they had no one to call who could help.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: Well, I would say, did you know that there was essentially one lawsuit for every four people? And they would say, no, I didn't know that.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: All these suits on this block.

segments.speaker: Latanya Graves
segments.text: Oh, on this block?

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: On this street.

segments.speaker: Latanya Graves
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This is a neighborhood where one in four people had been sued, and nobody knows that they're not the only one.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: Definitely nobody knew. [CHUCKLES] Nobody knew the numbers, and definitely, there was universal surprise at how prevalent it was.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Paul stopped by a brick bungalow, Cori Winfield's house. Only it's not her house anymore, because Cori lost the house to foreclosure after the car loan. segments.speaker: Rosalyn Turner
segments.text: Yes. After they started garnishing me, Walmart gave me a number to call. And I called them, and they wouldn't tell me much.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And Paul learned something else.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: She had been sued by Midwest Acceptance, as well. It was the same company that Cori had been sued by.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Who used to live in the same house.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: Who used to live in the same house. So it was like, jeez.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Rosalyn didn't know about Cori. Cori didn't know about Rosalyn. Paul was giving an entire neighborhood a status update on itself. Not that he'd set out to do that, but there he was, letting people know where they stood, relative to one another, even sometimes within the same family.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: It happened twice where I was like, who is X? And they're like, oh, that's my daughter. I was like, do you remember them dealing with a lawsuit from so-and-so? No. I mean, I found that-- yeah, even in the same house, people don't know.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Like here, in Dora Byrd's house. Paul asks, who's Camille Lee?

segments.speaker: Dora Byrd
segments.text: That's my granddaughter. What's Camille Lee got to do with-- what's going on with that?

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: Uh, sorry.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: In this one family, Dora Byrd had been sued for debt, her daughter had been sued for debt-- now she was learning her granddaughter had been sued for debt. Dora Byrd would try to help her granddaughter, now that she knows, but it will be hard, because a third of Dora's savings was garnished, too.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: On his last day in Jennings, Paul stopped by a brick house with three lawsuits.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: Yeah, so I went and knocked on the door, and a woman answered the second time we tried.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Miranda Jones. She welcomed him in.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: We went around her backyard. Then I learned that she is a councilwoman. She's a council member in Jennings, which was a surprise.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Although it made sense, given the fact that she seemed to be commanding various operations by cellphone on a Saturday.

segments.speaker: Miranda Jones
segments.text: It's on my desk. It's on my desk.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Paul tells Councilwoman Jones about his data.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: She said, you know, you should talk to the mayor. And so she texted the mayor while I was talking to her.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The mayor called right back.

segments.speaker: Miranda Jones
segments.text: Hey, Yolanda. Hey. I got a question for you. So there's a reporter that knocked on my door. He's from the--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The mayor said she'd be happy to meet Paul in her office.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: And then I drove right over to City Hall.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They sat down in the council chambers.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: I thought we were going to have like a kind of broader, 30,000-foot-- sort of the broader issues, like, what is this doing to my community as mayor? Like, that's the conversation that I thought we were going to have.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And what happened?

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: So we started that way, and then she just kind of casually threw in the conversation that "I've been sued by the sewerage district, too."

segments.speaker: Yolanda Henderson
segments.text: I'm going to be honest with you. I was one of the ones that was sued, as well, falling behind because I didn't have-- you know, I lost my job.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: And I tried not to-- I don't think I reacted in any way, because I try not to. But yeah, I was surprised, and I was-- it's almost like unbelievable at this point. And then at that point, I turned around and I wrote down the names that I saw, like on the name-- so we were in the city council chambers. It shows what all the names of all the city council members are. So I wrote all their names down and I was like, OK, when I get home, I'm going to look at the database and see how many city council members had actually been sued.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How many?

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: So it was five of the eight city council members had been sued over a debt. It's to the point where, yeah, it's unbelievable how common it is.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This should not be unbelievable by this point, right? Because Paul knows the data, has walked the streets. He's stared at the map. But still, it feels unbelievable. To the mayor, too, the mayor who has detailed knowledge of this particular community, who has experienced this herself. When Paul showed her her own block on his laptop?

segments.speaker: Yolanda Henderson
segments.text: Wow. See, that's my neighbor across the street. [INAUDIBLE] is right--

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: You get a sense that literally like--

segments.speaker: Yolanda Henderson
segments.text: Every other house.

segments.speaker: Paul Kiel
segments.text: Yeah. It's funny--

segments.speaker: Yolanda Henderson
segments.text: They're just suing all of us.

segments.text: "They're Just Suing All of Us." That was the front-page headline of the St. Louis Post Dispatch . Paul wrote a story for the paper about all this last month. segments.speaker: Yolanda Henderson
segments.text: It was kind of like-- it was sad, but then it was kind of like a relief. Because I'm like, oh my goodness, you know?

segments.text: I heard this from a few people. Now that they know their neighbors are in the same situation, they still don't want to talk about it. It's embarrassing. segments.text: And Mayor Henderson had some questions about what that meant, which she was too embarrassed to ask, for weeks. The mayor. Not some disempowered nobody-- the mayor. It wasn't until she was giving me a tour of City Hall that she decided to finally stop by the finance office again.

segments.text: All right. She's going to interview-- I got to ask you a question. My question is, on the MSD part, is it every pay period, or once a month, that 25% taken out of my pay?

segments.text: Every pay period. Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Yolanda Henderson
segments.text: See, if that's the case, that's not right. That's two weeks, every two weeks. That's $300 and some. Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It is standard. Unsurprising. That was actually the most consistent reason people gave for why they don't talk about this. It wasn't that surprising.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They did find it surprising when they learned how many of their neighbors had been garnished. But then, just a few minutes later, it stopped feeling surprising. segments.text: Act Four, 76-year-old Quarterback Throws Hail Mary Pass. OK, everybody. To close out show right now, I have an actual status update, a real-life status update, on somebody who was on our show a few weeks ago that many of you have written to us asking about.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: If you heard our show a few weeks ago, we had this 76-year-old man who wanted to ask this woman to marry him. He'd been visiting her for years, flying across the country to see her. He would stay at her house, hang out with her as friends, though he always wanted to be more than friends.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And he'd had a crush on this woman since he was the age of those girls you heard at the beginning of our program today, since high school. This girl he was about to ask to marry him was very relevant back then.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: She was very popular. She was one of, you might say, the queens in high school, right?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do you know where you're going to do this? Do you know where you're going to ask the question?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah, I know where and when.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Where is it going to be? What can you say about that?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: At her home. Next week.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And right before he left to fly and ask her the big question, he changed his plan. He decided that instead of asking her to marry him, he would just tell her his feelings and ask her if she wanted to be in a real committed relationship with him.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And he did it. And OK, I'm just going to cut to the chase. She turned him down. Turned him down flat. No interest at all.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She'd been married for 50 years. She didn't want it again, with him or anybody. Her life was full of friends. Didn't need it. That's what she said. Though, of course, that's basically the senior citizen way of saying, you know, it's not you, it's me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He says, right at the beginning of his visit, he got a sign of where her feelings were when he made the suggestion for the week together.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I said, the one thing I would like to do is to shut down the evening, if you didn't mind, by just dancing together, closing the evening down with maybe just 15 minutes or so of dancing. She didn't agree to that. She said, well, I'm not certain about that. That's something I'll have to think about.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: And of course, she didn't agree to that. And I know why. She didn't want any emotions to be involved, perhaps even her own, you know?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He was less sad about it than you might think, because he finally knew the truth, knew it was hopeless with her. He could move on. And he's kind of excited to move on. He says he knows now. If you meet somebody who's truly right for you, it shouldn't take years for both of you to recognize it and feel it.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: And if you don't, then it's time to cut it and run.
